extracted.intended_audience: fiction and narrative authors preparing manuscript beta reads (indie and traditionally-published writers seeking targeted reader feedback)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for authors on what to ask beta readers and how to structure beta-reading requests to get useful, actionable reader-perspective feedback on a manuscript (opening, plot clarity, characters, ending, mechanics, genre conventions, and author-specific concerns).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use structured feedback (targeted questions + broad invites)
rubrics_metrics.description: Structured feedback means asking a list of carefully chosen questions. This is good for you and good for your beta readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give beta readers a written list of questions (online form or Word document) and ask them to respond to each one. Structure helps readers who aren't professional editors know what to focus on and ensures nothing is missed; you can still invite spontaneous answers by including broader questions alongside targeted ones. Turn form responses into PDFs for easy reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate beta readers from professional editors
rubrics_metrics.description: Beta readers are typically ordinary readers with little or no expertise on story craft or publishing and are not here to tell you whether your plot conforms to a three-act structure, whether your characters have enough internal conflict, or whether your book can succeed in the current commercial market.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Save craft/market/editor-level questions for a professional editor. Instead, ask beta readers for the reader's perspective (what they connected with, where they lost interest, whether the ending satisfied them).

rubrics_metrics.name: Core overall-impression questions (always ask these three)
rubrics_metrics.description: Start by trying to gain a broad understanding of what your beta readers liked and didn’t like. We always ask these three questions to begin with: What was your overall impression of the story? What did you like about it the most? Was there anything you didn’t like about it? If so, what?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The first question elicits a top-line answer; the second and third invite slightly more detail about positives and negatives. These should be the opening questions before drilling down.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beginning engagement and pacing questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Did the story grab you at the beginning? Were there any points where you started to lose interest?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these to determine whether opening scenes need more energy or whether pacing lags in specific sections that require tightening or reworking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot clarity, coherence, and believability questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Was the story easy to follow? If not, why not? Was there anything particular that you found confusing? Was there anything you had trouble believing or that seemed illogical? Did you notice any inconsistencies in the plot, with the characters, or with anything else?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These questions identify confusing, convoluted, unbelievable, or inconsistent aspects of the story that need to be addressed. Ask for specifics (page/scene) where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character engagement and tracking questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Did you find the main character engaging? If so, what was most engaging about them? If you didn’t find them engaging, why not? Overall, which characters did you find the most engaging, and why? Overall, which characters did you find the least engaging, and why? Were you able to keep track of the characters, i.e. who was who? Were there too many?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure you get feedback about the protagonist and other key characters, including who resonated and whether the cast is clear or overcrowded. Ask for examples of moments that built or undermined engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ending satisfaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Did you find the ending satisfying?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This single, all-important question checks whether the resolution lands emotionally and logically for readers; include it among core questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanics: grammar, punctuation, spelling, formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask about the general standard of grammar, punctuation, spelling, and formatting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is useful to know for the author, but such mechanical feedback should be considered separately from reader-perspective story issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre-focused questions (conventions and expectations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every genre has its own conventions and expectations, so include genre-focused questions. For fantasy, ask about worldbuilding; for historical fiction, the authenticity of your setting; for romance, the level of spice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor a small set of targeted genre questions so readers can comment on how well you meet or subvert genre expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author-specific/targeted questions (place at end)
rubrics_metrics.description: There may be specific things about your story you’d like beta readers to reflect on (a scene, plot point, or character feature). The best place for questions like this is at the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a concern doesn't come up spontaneously earlier in feedback, it may not be a priority. Use targeted questions to check anxieties, and place them at the end to see if the issue surfaced organically in earlier answers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market/positioning/title/comparative questions (optional)
rubrics_metrics.description: You could ask whether beta readers would like to see a sequel, what books they think your story is comparable to, and whether they like your title or prefer an alternative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These questions help with positioning, finding comparable titles for blurbs/querying, and making title decisions; include them as optional extras.

rubrics_metrics.name: Look for patterns across readers; treat single dissent as outlier
rubrics_metrics.description: One huge benefit of using beta readers is that you can establish patterns. If one beta reader doesn’t connect to your main character, but all of the others do, that one is an outlier and you probably shouldn’t rewrite purely on that opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize issues flagged by multiple readers. Use frequency and common threads as the main signal for change; single responses can be noted but deprioritized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specify expected response length and adapt question count to reader type
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask beta readers to aim for a few sentences for each question, on average, to ensure you get enough detail. Be mindful that volunteers may feel overwhelmed by too many questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use paid readers or swapping-writer arrangements for longer/more numerous questions; with volunteers, consider limiting to ~10 questions or allow them to answer as many as they feel comfortable answering. State expectations up front.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order questions from broad to specific
rubrics_metrics.description: Start with broad, open questions to get spontaneous impressions, then narrow into specific elements you need to know about.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This ordering lets you capture top-line reactions before readers are guided into particular issues, and helps you spot whether targeted concerns came up naturally earlier.
